story_text.value:
Almost a year has passed since Desbordante’s last release, and now we’re rolling out a new one — 2.5.0.

Desbordante is an open-source, high-performance data profiler that finds and validates complex patterns in data using a bunch of advanced algorithms.

Unlike the black-box ML approaches that dominate today, Desbordante takes a symbolic, explainable approach to data analysis, producing explicit rules or rule-shaped artifacts that are verifiable, such as data dependencies, association rules, or other patterns. It’s a different way to analyze data, and it works well alongside black-box models. Unlike free-form model output, these patterns have precise semantics and can be validated algorithmically against the data. And, importantly, no hallucinations or misclassification.

This release adds 9 new patterns, including support for another dataset type: sequences in data. That brings the total to 4. We also picked up Python 3.15, which just came out. On top of the new patterns, there was a lot of infrastructure work too — mostly invisible to users, but important.

Full changelog: https://github.com/Desbordante/desbordante-core/releases/tag...

title.value: Show HN: Desbordante 2.5.0 Released

story_text.value:
I started using this a little over half a year ago to help me navigate through some large AI coded PRs people were submitting, because I felt like if I looked at the PR on Github I would just auto pass it through because I didn't want to deal with it. Thought I'd clean it up and share it in case this style of review was useful to anyone else.

Obviously it relies on an LLM run to get true semantic groupings of what changes were done, and why, but can also be used without an LLM to get more mechanical groupings/group names of changes made, along with the right order to view them in. The manual tree-sitter parsed analysis is deliberately conservative for now, but if people want to avoid the LLM analysis I can spend more time on that.

You can use it for other peoples PRs, or for your own when you've relied heavily on Claude Code or Codex for that particular PR. If the change came from your own Claude Code or Codex session, it reads your prompts and marks which changes you asked for and which the agent decided on its own as well to help you validate it before submitting for others to review.

Demo video done on some public project PRs is in the repo; for a look at what it looks like when it pulls in information about your own claude/codex sessions you'll have to use it yourself for now, but I'll work on getting an example of that up soon so people can take a look before spending time to get this to work locally for themselves.

I also added support for perforce style side by side diffing because I always kind of liked it, though it's not quite as slick yet.

title.value: Show HN: Perspica – A semantic diff for reviewing code

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Mark. Companies are really pushing cloud agents, but I found myself wanting to run agents on my Mac off-hours on my existing Claude/Codex subs.

I'd hit my usage limit coding with Fable, but not my limit on other models for tasks like marketing, research and content creation. So I built an orchestrator that organizes my agents into departments (or ships) where they have overriding goals/milestones and a "captain" agent can spawn other agents working in that department.

I think this structure works better than individual agent workers in an office. (Mundler Difflin)

The user can prompt the agent dispatcher for one-off or recurring tasks, which can be controlled from a Slack or a Telegram bot. Since Overboard has context about all your local projects it knows where it should spawn an agent. You can also talk to department heads or the main agent to see what human blockers are stalling projects, or give new direction for a department. Would love to hear feedback about the project. It's not open-source but there is a 14 day trial so anyone can test if it's useful before buying a license. (one-time $49)

story_text.value:
Upfront caveat: it's English only! but I'm personally still just amazed that 34MB (fine-tuned BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 ) can fit so much knowledge that it's possible to have an iPhone 15 running these classifications entirely client-side on arbitrary english text in 10-30ms.

The game is a little trivial but thought it was a cool showcase, you type messages to the guard and they get classified as either friendly, bribe, threats, etc.

I've been playing a lot with Jev use-cases since it came out and then learned about fine-tuning my own models.

The way I went about it was just using Jev first via a proxy to record my calls and store them as my own training data to make running training easier. I built a whole oss platform around doing that with models (of various sizes) https://github.com/doppsh/dopp.

Would love to hear any feedback / discuss more on either that whole training process or the game itself.

Also I did get a ton of help from Opus doing all this, so some things might be a little rough around some edges but plenty of human time has been put in too. Very welcoming of any feedback/criticism

story_text.value:
I created an open source alternative to tools like Instantly or Smartlead, which charge huge amounts of money per lead for basic cold email campaign management.

The emails are sent from your inbox, and you get open rates and analytics for your campaign.

It also comes with an MCP server, so you can manage the whole campaign from Claude or Codex.

It also has multi email option, so you can spread the senders through various emails as you like, and many other things like classification of replies or automatic draft reply generation.

If you like the project, you can sign up and use the hosted version and if you star the Github project it would help it grow!

Let me know what you think :)

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built Ciao to solve problems I was experiencing:

1. Connecting to a new host should be as seamless as possible. I SSH a lot nowadays, and I find the key sharing across devices cumbersome.

2. I get annoyed by setting up insert-your-favorite VPN on new machines. They're all great. I don't want to think about them.

3. There's a lot of harnesses: Claude Code and Codex now have decent mobile push notifications but what about Pi or xyz-shiny-new harness? The harness is another tool that should be abstracted out.

4. I want a single application that has the big picture of all of my agents. Tmux and Herdr are great but they don't have an overview of all my connected machines' agents.

---

With Ciao you curl|sh the daemon --> run ciao pair --> point your phone's camera at the QR code --> and you're connected. It uses iroh for accountless and E2EE connection. There's an optional relay server for APNS which too is E2EE.

One of my favorite aspects of agentic-engineering is being able to just have a lot of fun with programming. Among many features, I built a visually pleasing toggle between terminal-mode and native-chat-mode. If you install Ciao, come back here and tell me what you think.

---

Full transparency: this is a repost from yesterday, it was a massive day in AI.
